title: LEOTherm: from a simulation task to an analysis report
text: Welcome to LEOTherm, a thermal simulation workbench for low Earth orbit satellite research. Version one point two point one starts in English. This introduction uses the actual application, computed results and generated reports. We will start from an example, run a thermal simulation, explore optional stages, and finish with a report that records what was calculated.

title: Start with a template or a saved project
text: The Quick start page provides ready to use templates, a task wizard and saved projects. For a first run, choose First simulation. The wizard asks for a task name, duration and output interval. You can also copy a readable template and change a few fields. The Windows executable needs free MATLAB Runtime twenty twenty one b. Source users start the application with launch underscore g u i.

title: Define the orbit, attitude and heat sources
text: On Simulation, review the start time, duration, orbit altitude, inclination and orbit direction. Select the satellite attitude, then enable direct sunlight, reflected sunlight and Earth infrared radiation as needed. Check the displayed units. Warmup orbits reduce the influence of starting temperatures. Periodic convergence checks whether repeated orbits have reached a stable thermal cycle. The example network is a reference model, so mission specific studies need their own parameters.

title: Describe how satellite parts store and exchange heat
text: The thermal network represents satellite parts as connected temperature nodes. Set heat capacity, optical properties, internal power and thermal links. The solver calculates heat entering the satellite, heat exchanged between parts and heat radiated to space. It then integrates the temperature of each part over time. Receiver, antenna and oscillator roles help identify the response channels used in derived analyses.

title: Check the task, run it, and inspect the temperatures
text: Check the task before running. Required inputs are checked for the stages you selected. The basic nodal simulation always runs. In this example, the two hour task actually completed and passed its numerical checks. Temperature and illumination plots show the response through sunlight and shadow. The Results and export page provides the run status and report controls. Numerical acceptance means the declared checks passed; measured satellite data are needed to test physical agreement.

title: Compare several orbital conditions
text: Enable Parameter sweep when you want to compare conditions within one task. This demonstration runs six cases: two altitudes and three target beta angles. Beta describes the angle between the Sun direction and the orbital plane. Another mode varies dates, inclinations and orbit directions directly. Check each case status before comparing temperature ranges. These short demonstration runs include starting transients and do not establish a global optimum.

title: Use surface and volume meshes for detailed heat flow
text: The geometry stage accepts a surface model and a tetrahedral volume mesh. Declare mesh units, material properties, contacts and thermal boundaries. This example actually runs surface to volume coupling: calculated surface heat loads drive internal conduction. The current coupling is one way and requires matching boundary geometry. The task report is the source for the newly computed results; the geometry panel may still display an older result. Inspect heat flow accounting as well as temperatures.

title: Bring an existing thermal model into the task
text: Engineering thermal model exchange provides a route for reusing existing models. Import a supported exchange file, inspect it, define the node mapping and preview the changes before applying them. Custom adapters and external solver interfaces are available to developers. A successful file import checks the declared format. Units, materials and boundaries still need to represent the intended device. This introduction shows the exchange interface, not a commercial solver execution.

title: Compare the simulation with temperature measurements
text: Telemetry and validation maps time, measured temperatures and their corresponding model nodes. Check the time span, units, missing values and exact time alignment before comparing results. This demonstration runs the built in synthetic example, which teaches the workflow and is not an in orbit validation. For your satellite, use traceable measurements and independently held out days. The report includes the scored comparison and its limits. Missing data are not silently interpolated.

title: Fit parameters within realistic device limits
text: Device calibration uses nominal device parameters, explicit allowed ranges and penalties for moving away from the reference values. Split whole days into training, validation and test sets. Only accepted fitted parameters should drive a later simulation. This screen explains the configuration; no new calibration fit is claimed in this introduction. Use separate test data to judge agreement, and review the warnings before treating a fit as a validated device model.

title: Read the task-specific analysis report
text: The final analysis report is the main deliverable. It records the task settings, temperature statistics, calculated response metrics and numerical acceptance. Each completed optional stage adds its own findings, charts and tables. Skipped stages are identified in the stage record. Interpret the findings together with the model assumptions and warmup checks. The reports shown here were generated by the actual base, sweep, geometry and telemetry tasks.

title: Keep the complete run and repeat the study
text: Each run also retains the input snapshot, frozen model, computed data and stage status. Save the project to continue your work, then run changed settings in a new directory so earlier evidence remains available. Start with the simple template, add only the stages you need, and finish by reading the report. The language selector still supports Chinese. Your saved project remembers its language and configuration.
